title: Time Unit Ladder
context: Grade 4, and the chapter's topic on changing one unit of time into another. An adult sees a multiplication, which it is. What is actually being settled is which number to multiply by, twenty-four for days and sixty for hours and for minutes, and what happens to the part already in the smaller unit. A child who multiplies every number in sight turns three hours forty minutes into far too many minutes, and one who drops the forty answers one hundred and eighty. The printed questions name the unit they want, so the unit is part of the answer.

writeup.why: Know how many of each unit of time make the next, and change days, hours or minutes into a smaller unit, with the part already there added on.
writeup.look: A ladder of four rungs, day, hour, minute and second, with tiles on the rungs, and a clock with a thin second hand beside it.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Time Unit Ladder' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the tiles opened against the tiles this phase lays out, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each tile opens and the second fixed at what this phase holds. On the first phase it counts the laps of the second hand against the laps asked for, and on the second the tags filled against three. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The ladder stands at the left of the working area, 600 by 460 at 76,222, with four rungs one above another, each 560 wide and 90 tall, labelled at their left ends from the top: day, hour, minute and second. Day tiles are olive, hour tiles and cells vermilion, minute tiles and cells deep blue, and second cells reddish purple. Between each pair of rungs, at the right end, sits an exchange tag, 80 by 40, blank until it is filled: twenty-four between day and hour, sixty between hour and minute, and sixty between minute and second. A time is loaded as tiles on its rungs, one tile for each unit. The step down control, 160 by 56 at 700,226, opens every tile on a rung into cells on the rung below: an hour tile opens into a bar of sixty minute cells in six rows of ten, a minute tile into sixty second cells the same way, and a day tile into twenty-four hour cells in two rows of ten and four more. Past three bars on a rung, each full bar folds into a neat stack at the rung's right end with the number of bars written beside it. As the tiles open, the multiplication for the whole rung is written beside it in ink, the number of tiles times the exchange, with the total after it. The side bay, 200 by 200 at 880,226, holds any tiles already in the smaller unit until the slide control under it, 200 by 56 at 880,436, brings them in beside the opened cells. The add bar runs under the ladder, 600 by 44 at 76,686, and writes the total of the rung it is set on. The second hand clock stands at the lower right, a face 200 across centred at 1010,610, with a vermilion hour hand, a deep blue minute hand and a thin reddish purple second hand. It ticks one mark a second, counts its ticks beside it, and steps the minute hand on one mark at the end of each lap. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve keys three across, the ten digits and two keys that clear and go back, with a unit strip under the slot reading days, hours, minutes and seconds, and the answer slot will not settle a number until the unit the question asks for is chosen. On the second phase a word pad of the four unit names sits over it for ordering the rungs. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The hour hand, every hour tile and hour cell, the hours column, and the hours of a time the stage splits into hours and minutes are vermilion. The minute hand, every minute tile and minute cell, the minutes column and the minutes of a split time are deep blue. The second hand, every second cell and the seconds column are reddish purple. The a.m. half of the day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue on every strip, timeline and track, and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber, so the label changes where the colour does. Time counted between a start and an end, every hop and total on a track, and the days counted between two dates are green. An hour or a minute carried or broken, with the digits it strikes and rewrites, is wine. A calendar day, week or year picked out or ticked, a month on its bar and a day tile are olive. The days left over beyond whole weeks, and the twenty-ninth of February in a leap year, are yellow outlined in near-black. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every clock rim, minute mark, clock number, hub, rule, tick, post, bracket, guide line and panel edge is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because an hour hand is told from a minute hand by its length, a column by its heading, a half of the day by its label, and a counted day from one left out by being filled rather than outlined, before any of them is told by a colour. A figure that goes down by one is struck through once with the new figure written above it, and never rubbed out. A bar of sixty cells is drawn as six rows of ten and a day's hour cells as two rows of ten and four, so no bar on this stage can be read as a hundred. Tiles already in the smaller unit are not multiplied: they wait in the side bay and are slid in and added.
writeup.finish: The card shows the ladder with the child's last time opened down its rungs, the multiplication and the added part written beside it, and the answer with its unit.

phases.win: sixty ticks are counted, and the minute hand steps on exactly one mark
phases.does: starts the second hand and counts its ticks for one whole lap, watching the minute hand
phases.goal: the second hand moves one mark each second and goes round once a minute, so one minute is sixty seconds
phases.says: Watch the thin hand go all the way round. How many ticks is that? What did the minute hand do?
phases.check: Away from the screen: the second hand goes round twice. How many seconds is that, and how many minutes?
phases.feels: one lap of the thin hand is sixty ticks, and the long hand creeps one mark for it
phases.hands: Watch a real second hand go round once with the class counting each tick aloud, and stop at sixty. Ask what the minute hand did while that happened. Then run it for two laps and ask how many seconds passed.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many marks are there round the face? Second rung, the phase's: how long does the second hand take to pass one mark? Third rung: the clock is cut to one stretch from one number to the next, five ticks, before the whole lap comes back. The pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the numbers are what stand out on a face, and counting them is quicker than counting marks.
wrong.move: counts the twelve numbers as the second hand passes them, and says one lap is twelve seconds.
wrong.screen: the second hand is run again from the twelve, and the tick count beside the clock climbs by one at every mark, reaching five at the one, ten at the two, and sixty back at the twelve. The minute hand steps on one mark as the lap ends, and the child's twelve stays in the slot beside the count.

wrong.why: the minute hand is read in fives from the numbers, so its steps seem to go from number to number.
wrong.move: says one lap of the second hand moves the minute hand on to the next number, five minutes.
wrong.screen: the second hand runs one lap and the tick count writes sixty, and the minute hand's move is lit: one small mark and no further. A second lap steps it one more mark, and the child's answer stays in the slot beside the two marks.

phases.screen: the clock with three hands, the thin second hand at the twelve, and a count of ticks at nought
phases.soWhat: The second hand goes round once every minute, so one minute is sixty seconds.

phases.win: the rungs settle as day, hour, minute and second, and twenty-four, sixty and sixty fill the tags
phases.does: orders the rungs from the largest unit at the top to the smallest at the bottom, then fills each exchange tag
phases.goal: sixty seconds make a minute, sixty minutes make an hour and twenty-four hours make a day, with the second the smallest and the hour the largest of the three
phases.says: How many of the smaller unit make one of the bigger one?
phases.check: Which is larger, an hour or a minute? How many of the smaller make the larger?
phases.feels: each unit is a bundle of the one below it, and the day's bundle is a different size from the others
phases.hands: Write four cards, day, hour, minute and second, and have four children stand holding them in order from the largest to the smallest. Between each pair the class says how many of the smaller make one of the larger, and writes it on a slip held between them.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which of these units is the smallest? Second rung, the phase's: how many of the smaller unit make one of the next? Third rung: the ladder is cut to two rungs, minute and second, and the child fills their one tag before the other rungs come back. The word pad and the number pad stay open.

wrong.why: sixty is said twice going up the ladder, so it sounds like the number for every step.
wrong.move: uses sixty for every step, and says a day is sixty hours.
wrong.screen: the child's sixty is set on the tag between day and hour, and a day tile is stepped down: its cells fill two rows of ten and four more, and the rung stops there at twenty-four, with the child's tag still reading sixty beside the count. The child's answer stays in the slot, nothing marked.

wrong.why: sixty looks bigger than one, and the size of a number is easy to take for the size of the unit.
wrong.move: puts the second above the minute, because sixty seconds is a bigger number than one minute.
wrong.screen: one minute tile is set on the minute rung and stepped down, and it opens into sixty second cells, each far smaller than the tile. The sixty cells are laid back over the minute tile and fill it exactly, and the child's order stays set out beside the ladder.

phases.screen: the ladder with its four rungs in a jumble and the three exchange tags blank
phases.soWhat: Sixty seconds make a minute, sixty minutes make an hour, and twenty-four hours make a day.

phases.win: every tile opens into the rung below, and the multiplication and the total are written beside it
phases.does: steps the tiles down, watches each open into the smaller unit, and writes the multiplication for the whole row
phases.goal: a larger unit is changed into a smaller one by multiplying by the number between their rungs
phases.says: Each of these breaks into how many of the next? So how many are there in all?
phases.check: How many hours are there in six days? And how many minutes in six hours?
phases.feels: every tile on the rung opens into the same number of cells, so a row of tiles is one multiplication
phases.hands: Draw three large squares on the board for three hours, and fill one with six rows of ten dots while the class counts. Ask how many dots the other two hold without drawing them, and write three times sixty. Then ask how many hours are in two days, and write two times twenty-four.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which rung are the tiles on, and which rung is below it? Second rung, the phase's: how many cells does one tile open into? Third rung: the row is cut to one tile, and the child opens it and counts its cells before the full row comes back. The pad and the unit strip stay open.

wrong.why: hours and minutes both use sixty, and the day's twenty-four is the one exchange on the ladder that differs.
wrong.move: multiplies nine days by sixty and answers five hundred and forty hours.
wrong.screen: the nine day tiles step down one at a time, and each opens into two rows of ten hour cells and four more, twenty-four and no more. The multiplication beside the rung is written nine times twenty-four, and the total two hundred and sixteen. The child's five hundred and forty stays in the slot beside it.

wrong.why: a metre is a hundred centimetres, and a hundred is the round number that comes to mind for how many small units make a big one.
wrong.move: writes three hours as three hundred minutes, as if an hour were a hundred minutes the way a metre is a hundred centimetres.
wrong.screen: the three hour tiles step down, and each opens into a bar of sixty minute cells in six rows of ten, not ten rows of ten. The three bars make one hundred and eighty. The child's three hundred is laid beside them in bars of sixty and runs to five bars, which is five hours, and the child's number stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a row of tiles on one rung, with the rung below empty
phases.soWhat: To change a larger unit into a smaller one, multiply by the number of small units in one large one.

phases.win: the two groups of minutes join into one row, and the total is written in minutes
phases.does: steps the hour tiles down, slides the side bay's minutes in, and writes the total with its unit
phases.goal: a time in two units is changed into the smaller unit by changing the larger part and adding the part already there
phases.says: Break the hours into minutes first. Now, what about the minutes that were already there?
phases.check: Change four hours twenty minutes into minutes. What did you multiply, and what did you add?
phases.feels: the hours need changing and the minutes do not, so the two parts are treated differently
phases.hands: Write two hours twenty minutes on the board and change it into minutes with the class in two steps: the hours into minutes first, sixty and sixty, then the twenty that were minutes already added on. Ask why the twenty were not multiplied. Then write one hour thirty minutes and ask someone to say it as minutes aloud.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which part of the time is in the larger unit? Second rung, the phase's: what happens to the part already in the smaller unit? Third rung: the time is cut to one hour and a few minutes, and the child opens the hour and slides the minutes in before the larger time comes back. The pad and the unit strip stay open.

wrong.why: the multiplying is the work, and once it is done the small part looks as if it has been dealt with.
wrong.move: leaves out the eighteen minutes and answers three hundred minutes for five hours eighteen minutes.
wrong.screen: the five hour tiles open into five bars of sixty, three hundred cells, and the side bay's eighteen minute tiles glow and slide in beside them. The add bar writes three hundred and eighteen, and the child's three hundred stays in the slot beside it.

wrong.why: one hour thirty looks like one and thirty side by side, and a one in front of thirty makes a hundred and thirty.
wrong.move: writes one hour thirty minutes as one hundred and thirty minutes, reading the time as a whole number.
wrong.screen: the hour tile opens into one bar of sixty, and the thirty from the side bay slide in beside it: ninety. The child's one hundred and thirty is laid beside it in bars of sixty, two full bars and ten more, which is two hours ten minutes, and the child's number stays in the slot.

wrong.why: a time of sixty or more minutes is often turned into hours and minutes, and that move is easy to make when the question asks for something else.
wrong.move: for eighty-five minutes in seconds, writes one hour twenty-five minutes, changing the time up the ladder instead of down.
wrong.screen: the child's answer is built first: sixty of the eighty-five minute cells gather into one hour tile that rises a rung, and the twenty-five left over stay on the minute rung as minutes, which is what going up the ladder gives. The unit strip then lights seconds, the unit the question asks for, and the eighty-five minutes step down instead, each opening into sixty second cells: eighty-five times sixty, five thousand one hundred seconds. The child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a time loaded as hour tiles and minute tiles, with the minute tiles waiting in the side bay
phases.soWhat: For a time in two units, change the larger unit, then add the part already in the smaller unit.

writeup.delight: The third phase, when one day tile is stepped down twice. It opens into twenty-four hour cells, and stepping those down opens each into a bar of sixty minute cells, until the minute rung is lined with folded stacks and the multiplication beside it reads twenty-four times sixty, one thousand four hundred and forty minutes, all out of one small olive tile. It can be run as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the clock beside the ladder shows its thin second hand at the twelve and the tick count at nought, and the ladder stands dim. On the second the four rungs lie in a jumble at the foot of the ladder and the three exchange tags between the rung places are blank. On the third a row of tiles stands on one rung with the rung below it empty. On the fourth hour tiles stand on the hour rung and minute tiles wait in the side bay. The running count at the top left holds the tiles opened against the tiles this phase lays out, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the second hand, or the rung marked day, or the first tile, or the side bay, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks how many of each unit make the next. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any tiles on any rung, the step down control, the side bay, the add bar and the second hand clock all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the second hand, the three exchanges, changing a larger unit into a smaller one, and changing two units into one.
voiceLines: A ladder of units, from days down to seconds. How many of each make the next?
Watch the thin hand go all the way round. How many ticks is that? What did the minute hand do?
How many of the smaller unit make one of the bigger one?
Each of these breaks into how many of the next? So how many are there in all?
Break the hours into minutes first. Now, what about the minutes that were already there?
A new time. Say its unit before you step anything down.
Free play. Any tiles on any rung, with the step down, the side bay and the second hand open.
Open one tile and count what is inside it.
Each tile opened into the right number, the part already there added on, and each answer given its unit.

observations.why: The second hand moves one mark each second and there are sixty marks round the face, so one lap is one minute.
observations.soWhat: The second hand goes round once every minute, so one minute is sixty seconds.
observations.observe: Sixty ticks were counted in one lap, and the minute hand stepped on exactly one mark.

observations.why: Each unit is made of a number of the unit below it, and the day's number is twenty-four, not sixty.
observations.soWhat: Sixty seconds make a minute, sixty minutes make an hour, and twenty-four hours make a day.
observations.observe: The rungs settled with the day at the top and the second at the foot, and the tags read twenty-four, sixty and sixty.

observations.why: Every tile on a rung is one of the same unit, so each opens into the number on the tag below it.
observations.soWhat: To change a larger unit into a smaller one, multiply by the number of small units in one large one.
observations.observe: Each tile on the rung opened into the same number of cells, and the multiplication beside the rung gave the total.

observations.why: Those minutes were minutes already, so they needed no changing.
observations.soWhat: For a time in two units, change the larger unit, then add the part already in the smaller unit.
observations.observe: The side bay's minutes slid in beside the opened hours and were added, not opened.

source_tool.description: A ladder of four rungs stands in the working area, labelled from the top: day, hour, minute and second. Between each pair of rungs a tag gives the exchange, twenty-four hours in a day, sixty minutes in an hour and sixty seconds in a minute, and the tags start blank. A time is loaded as tiles on its rungs, so three hours forty minutes is three hour tiles and forty minute tiles. A step down control breaks every tile on a rung into the rung below. Each hour tile opens into a bar of sixty minute cells in six rows of ten, and each day tile into twenty-four hour cells. The multiplication for the whole rung is written beside it as the tiles open, the number of tiles times the exchange. Tiles already on the lower rung wait in a side bay and slide in after the step down, and an add bar writes the total. The answer slot carries the unit the question asks for and will not take a number without it. A clock with a thin second hand stands beside the ladder. It ticks one mark a second, and when the second hand completes a lap the minute hand steps on one mark.
source_tool.art_direction: A ladder of time units and tiles / Picture book

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a clock face with sixty marks, a strip of the day from one midnight to the next, a ladder of units with tiles, the page's own timeline, a column frame, a time track with flags and a hopper, and a wall of month cards.

Every clock is drawn exactly. The minute hand turns six degrees a minute and points exactly at a minute mark, and the hour hand turns thirty degrees an hour and half a degree a minute, so it sits exactly where the time puts it and never on a number except at the hour.

The minute hand is always the longer hand and the hour hand the shorter, and a second hand, where there is one, is the thinnest. A clock face always shows all twelve numbers and all sixty marks, with a longer mark at each number.
A time in figures is written with a colon and a.m. or p.m., as 4:40 p.m., and a 24-hour time as four digits and the word hours, as 1615 hours. Twelve o'clock is written 12 noon or 12 midnight.
Noon and midnight are drawn as posts wherever a strip, a timeline or a track crosses them, and a.m. changes to p.m., or back, only at a post.
A column of time carries at sixty. A carried or broken hour or minute is drawn as sixty cells in six rows of ten, never as ten or as a hundred.
A month card is the real month of the year shown, with its first day under the right weekday and the right number of days, as the calendar in use today lays out that year.
Every day count shows which of its ends it counts. A day that is counted is filled, and a day that is left out is outlined only, at full strength and never hidden.
Two answers being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one beside or above the other. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
A hand, a column, a flag or a day is told apart by its shape, its label and its place first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a digit, a tile, a cell or a day the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The hour hand, an hour tile, an hours column and the hours of a time split into hours and minutes are vermilion. The minute hand and every minute are deep blue, and the second hand and every second are reddish purple, following the page, whose hour hand is red and whose second hand is a thin pink. The a.m. half of the day, midnight to noon, is sky blue on every strip, timeline and track, and the p.m. half is amber, so the label changes where the colour does. Time counted between a start and an end, every hop and total on the duration track, and the days counted between two dates are green. An hour or a minute carried or broken, with the digits it strikes and rewrites, is wine. A calendar day, week or year picked out or ticked, a month on its bar and a day tile on the ladder are olive. The days left over beyond whole weeks, and the twenty-ninth of February in a leap year, are yellow outlined in near-black. Every clock rim, minute mark, number, hub, rule, tick, post, bracket and guide line is near-black chrome. All of that holds in greyscale, because an hour hand is told from a minute hand by its length, a column by its heading, a half of the day by its label, and a counted day from one left out by being filled rather than outlined.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Open one tile and count what is inside it.
voice.onNext: A new time. Say its unit before you step anything down.
voice.opening: A ladder of units, from days down to seconds. How many of each make the next?
voice.onFinish: Each tile opened into the right number, the part already there added on, and each answer given its unit.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any tiles on any rung, with the step down, the side bay and the second hand open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has watched a second hand go round for a whole minute, counting aloud, and has worked out how many minutes a short lesson lasts. The tool opens each hour tile into sixty minute cells in front of the child, so the sixty in the multiplication is seen rather than remembered. It keeps the minutes already there waiting to be added.

answer_key.rule: Sixty seconds make one minute, sixty minutes make one hour, and twenty-four hours make one day. The second is the smallest of the three clock units and the hour the largest, and a day is larger still. The second hand moves one mark each second and goes round once a minute. To change a larger unit into a smaller one, multiply: days by twenty-four to get hours, hours by sixty to get minutes, and minutes by sixty to get seconds. For a time in two units, change the larger unit and then add the part already in the smaller unit. So one hour twenty-five minutes is sixty minutes and twenty-five minutes, eighty-five minutes. Give the answer in the unit the question asks for.
answer_key.wrong: The step down runs again one tile at a time, each tile opening into its cells while they are counted, and the side bay's tiles are slid in last. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The second hand moves one mark each second, and there are sixty marks round the face.
So one lap is sixty seconds, and three laps are three sixties, one hundred and eighty seconds.
Each lap moves the minute hand on one mark, so three laps move it three marks, three minutes.
items.answer: One hundred and eighty seconds pass, and the minute hand moves three marks, which is three minutes
items.question: The second hand goes round the clock three times. How many seconds pass, and how far does the minute hand move?
items.checkpoint: The second hand goes round once every minute, so one minute is sixty seconds.
items.misconception: Counting the twelve numbers instead of the sixty marks, and saying one lap is twelve seconds.

steps: The second is the smallest: the second hand moves one mark for each one.
Sixty seconds make a minute, and sixty minutes make an hour.
A day is the largest of the four, and it is twenty-four hours, not sixty.
items.answer: A second, a minute, an hour, a day. Sixty seconds make a minute, sixty minutes make an hour, and twenty-four hours make a day
items.question: Put these units in order from the smallest to the largest: an hour, a second, a day, a minute. Say how many of each make the next.
items.checkpoint: Sixty seconds make a minute, sixty minutes make an hour, and twenty-four hours make a day.
items.misconception: Using sixty for every step, and saying a day is sixty hours.

steps: Each day is 24 hours, so 9 days are 9 times 24 hours.
180 and 36 make 216, so 9 days are 216 hours.
items.question: How many hours are there in 9 days?
items.checkpoint: To change a larger unit into a smaller one, multiply by the number of small units in one large one.
items.misconception: Multiplying by sixty because hours and minutes use sixty, and answering 540 hours.

steps: Change the hours first: 5 hours are 5 times 60, which is 300 minutes.
The 18 minutes are already minutes, so they are added on, not multiplied.
items.question: Change 5 hours 18 minutes into minutes.
items.checkpoint: For a time in two units, change the larger unit, then add the part already in the smaller unit.
items.misconception: Leaving out the 18 minutes and answering 300, or multiplying them by sixty as well.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: How many seconds are there in one minute, and which hand of a clock counts them?
items.final_answer: Sixty seconds, counted by the thin second hand

items.question: Which is the largest of these units: a minute, an hour or a second?
How many minutes are there in 3 hours?
How many seconds are there in 14 minutes?
A holiday class meets for 3 hours on each of 4 days. How many minutes of class is that in all?
items.final_answer: 720 minutes. The class meets for 12 hours in all, and 12 times 60 is 720

items.question: A film is 2 hours 52 minutes long. How many minutes is that?
items.final_answer: 172 minutes, because 2 hours are 120 minutes and 52 more are added

items.question: A song lasts 4 minutes 5 seconds. A child changes it and writes 245 minutes. What should the answer be?
items.final_answer: 245 seconds. The minutes were changed into seconds, so the answer is in seconds, not minutes

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: four rungs, day, hour, minute and second, from the top down
sit between the rungs and are filled with twenty-four, sixty and sixty
load a time onto its rungs, one tile for each unit
opens every tile on a rung into cells of the rung below and writes the multiplication
holds the tiles already on the lower rung until they are slid in and added
adds the opened cells and the side bay into one total
takes an answer only with the unit the question asks for
ticks one mark a second and steps the minute hand on at the end of each lap

teaching_notes: Before the tool is opened, watch a real second hand go round for a whole minute with the class counting aloud. Let them see the minute hand step on one mark as it finishes. The page names three units, the hour, the minute and the second, and uses the day as well, twenty-four hours. Say the three exchanges every time: twenty-four for days, sixty for hours and sixty for minutes. The worked examples change one unit at a time and then two units into one, and the second kind is where the added part is lost. Watch the exercise that asks for seventy-five minutes in seconds: it wants seconds, not an hour and fifteen minutes. The match in the On Your Own box is played for at most six hours a day. The page asks for its total minutes, so work it as five days of six hours. One exercise sets its conversion in a breathing exercise held for a long time. This plan does not reuse that setting, because breath-holding is not a safe thing for children to practise.
generation_prompt: Build a units of time tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A ladder of four rungs stands in the working area, labelled from the top day, hour, minute and second. A blank exchange tag between each pair of rungs is to be filled with twenty-four, sixty and sixty. A time is loaded as tiles on its rungs, one tile for each unit, and tiles on a lower rung wait in a side bay. A step down control opens every tile on a rung into cells of the rung below, and writes the multiplication for the whole rung beside it. The cells are drawn in rows of ten, so sixty read as six rows and twenty-four as two rows and four. A slide control brings the side bay's tiles in beside the opened cells, and an add bar writes the total. The answer slot fixed down the right of the canvas shows the unit the question asks for and will not settle a number without it. Beside the ladder stands a clock with an hour hand, a minute hand and a thin second hand. It ticks one mark a second, counts its ticks, and steps the minute hand on one mark after each lap. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Watch the second hand go round once. Fill in the numbers between the rungs. Step each tile down and multiply. Add on the part that was already there. Write the unit.
